title: Bags from Old Sails
focus: Inversion after negative adverbials (not only, never, hardly, only after)

lines.text: Diego, you started a business at nineteen. What does it sell?
Bags made from old sails and tents. Not only are they strong, but they also have a story.
Where did the idea come from?
My grandfather repaired boats. Never had I seen so many torn sails thrown away until I visited his workshop.
And how did you begin?
Hardly had I bought my first sewing machine when I realised I had no idea how to use it. A neighbour taught me.
Was it profitable straight away?
Not at all. Only after a year did I sell enough to pay myself a small wage.
What would you say to other young people with ideas?
Start small. Under no circumstances should you borrow a large sum before you've tested the market.
Do you ever think about expanding?
Yes, but carefully. Rarely do businesses fail because they're too slow; more often they grow too fast.

title: A Library That Lends Tools

lines.text: We're at the central library, where something unusual has been happening for the past six months.
That's right. We've been lending tools alongside books since the spring.
What kind of tools?
Drills, ladders, sewing machines, even a pasta maker. Most people only need them once or twice a year.
So why buy them?
Exactly. We've been trying to cut waste, and households save a lot of money too.
Has it been popular?
Far more than we'd expected. We've been receiving about thirty requests a week, and some tools are booked for months.
Any problems?
One or two. A few items have been returned late, and a ladder came back with a bent leg.
How do you deal with that?
We ask borrowers to sign a simple agreement, and we offer a short training session for the heavier equipment.
Will other libraries copy the idea?
I hope so. Two nearby towns have already been asking us for advice.

title: Seeing What We Expect
focus: Cause and result (so ... that, such ... that, as a result, consequently)

lines.text: Good afternoon. Today I'd like to explain a very common thinking error called confirmation bias.
It means that we tend to notice information that agrees with what we already believe, and ignore the rest.
Imagine you think a certain football team is unlucky. Every time they lose by a late goal, you remember it.
When they win comfortably, you forget it. As a result, your belief seems to be confirmed again and again.
The effect is so strong that even scientists must work hard to avoid it.
That is why good research is designed so that the result can be wrong. If a test can't fail, it proves nothing.
Social media makes the problem worse. The more we click on one kind of opinion, the more we're shown similar opinions.
Consequently, many people live in a bubble where nobody ever disagrees with them.
So what can we do? First, actively look for evidence against your own view.
Second, ask a friend who disagrees with you to explain why, and listen without interrupting.
It is such a simple habit that most people never try it. But it works surprisingly well.
For homework, find an article you disagree with and summarise its best argument fairly.

title: Allergy Rules in the Kitchen
focus: Obligation and necessity (must, have to, be required to, be allowed to)

lines.text: Before service, a quick briefing about allergies. Last week we nearly served a nut sauce to a guest who had told us about her allergy.
That's serious. What went wrong?
The order was written down, but the note wasn't passed to the kitchen. From now on, every allergy has to be shouted across the pass and repeated back.
So the waiter says it, and the cook repeats it?
Exactly. Nobody is allowed to start the dish until it's confirmed.
What about the shared chopping boards?
Good question. Separate boards must be used for any order with an allergy, and they have to be washed straight afterwards.
Do we need to change gloves as well?
Yes. Fresh gloves each time, and hands must be washed even if you're wearing gloves.
What if a customer isn't sure what's in a dish?
Don't guess. You're required to check with me, or with the sous chef, before answering.
Understood. Will we get written guidance?
Yes, a laminated card will be put up by each station tomorrow.
Brilliant. I'd feel much safer.

title: Is the Narrator Lying?
focus: Modals of speculation (must, can't, might, could, may well)

lines.text: Welcome to Page Turners. This month we read The Glass Orchard, and I have to say the ending divided our book club.
I loved it, but I'm still not sure what happened. The narrator must be hiding something.
I think she can't be telling the whole truth. Why would she describe the fire so calmly?
She might be in shock. People often stay oddly calm after a disaster.
Possible, but she told her sister that she hadn't been home that night. Then a neighbour says he saw her at the window.
So either the neighbour is mistaken or she's lying. He could have seen someone else.
It was dark, so he may well have been wrong. Yet he sounded very certain.
The author seems to want us to doubt everyone. Even the sister could be involved.
Do you think we're supposed to find an answer?
Probably not. If the writer had wanted to explain everything, she'd have written a detective story.
Fair. My vote is four stars, mainly for the atmosphere.
Three and a half from me. I couldn't stop thinking about it, though, which must count for something.
It does. Next month we read a collection of short stories, so bring suggestions.

title: Cars or Buses?
focus: Comparatives (the more ..., the less ...; as ... as; far, slightly)

lines.text: Tonight: should cities spend more on electric cars or on public transport? Ali first.
Public transport, without a doubt. The more people share a bus, the less energy each passenger uses.
But electric cars are far cleaner than petrol cars, and people like the freedom they give.
Cleaner, yes, but a city full of electric cars still has just as many traffic jams as before.
Not everyone lives near a bus route, though. In small towns, buses are nowhere near as frequent.
Then improve them. The better the service, the more people will choose it.
That takes years and a lot of money. Charging points can be installed much faster.
Fair, but it's slightly misleading to call that a solution if the roads stay full.
I'd say a mix is more realistic. Electric cars in the countryside, trains and buses in the centre.
Ali, can you accept a mix?
Provided the city centre is not given over to cars, yes.
So, a partial agreement. Thank you both.

title: Which Plan Is Better?

lines.text: Hi, can I help you with anything?

How much data do you normally use?
Not much. A few gigabytes a month, mainly for maps and messages.
Then you don't need our biggest plan. This one has plenty of data and costs eighteen pounds a month.
That's still a lot. Is there anything cheaper?
There's a smaller plan for twelve pounds, but it only includes a little data, so you might run out.
What happens if I do?
You pay a small extra charge for each extra gigabyte, so be careful with video.
I see. And the contract? I don't want to be tied down for too long.
Our plans last twelve months, but there's a thirty day trial where you can cancel with no fee.
That's reassuring. I'll try the smaller one, then. Is there enough signal in the countryside?
Generally yes, although there are a few areas with weak coverage. I'd check the map on our website.

title: A Night in an Ambulance

lines.text: Gareth, you've been a paramedic for twelve years. What's a typical night like?
There's no such thing. What makes the job interesting is that you never know what the next call will be.
What's the hardest part?
Waiting for the radio to ring while thinking about the people who might need us. And of course, the cases involving children.
How do you cope with stress?
We have a short debrief after difficult shifts, which helps. And I run, which clears my head.
Do people sometimes misunderstand your job?
Often. Many think we only deal with road accidents, but most of what we see is illness: chest pain, breathing problems, falls at home.
What advice would you give to the public?
Learn basic first aid. The people who act in the first few minutes often make the biggest difference.
And when should someone call an ambulance?
Whenever there's a serious risk to life, such as severe bleeding or a person who isn't breathing.
Do you ever think about changing careers?
Sometimes, after a bad night. But then someone thanks us, and I remember why I do it.

title: The Old Lighthouse Tour
focus: Past habits and passive voice (used to, would, was built, was written down)

lines.text: Welcome to the old lighthouse. Please keep to the left on the stairs, as they're quite narrow.
The tower was built in the middle of the nineteenth century, after several ships had been wrecked on the rocks below.
Before electricity arrived, the lamp was lit by hand every evening. The keeper would climb these stairs twice a day.
Keepers used to live here with their families, and the children went to a small school in the village.
Life wasn't easy. In winter, supplies could only be delivered when the sea was calm, so the keepers had to store food for months.
On the next floor you can see the keeper's logbook. Every storm and every passing ship was written down by hand.
In the nineteen seventies, the light was automated, and the last keeper left. Today, the building is looked after by volunteers.
If you're feeling energetic, there are more steps up to the lantern room. The view is worth it.
Please don't lean over the rail, and hold on to your children at the top.
Photos are welcome, but flash is not allowed inside the lamp room.
We'll meet again at the cafe at the bottom, where there's a short film about the rescues carried out from this station.
Thank you for visiting, and enjoy the tour.
